tutorial.title: Intro to Express Router
tutorial.descriptionContent: Learn what the Express router is and how to utilize it

lessons.title: Intro I
lessons.interactiveContent:
The Express router helps organize web application's routes into separate, manageable pieces.

The Express router keeps routes organized, making it easier to find and use them, just like putting toys in separate boxes!

lessons.title: Lesson #2
lessons.interactiveContent:
To use the Express router, we first need to require the Express module and then access the router.

Make sure to pick express, followed by .Router().

lessons.title: Lesson #3
lessons.interactiveContent:
We define routes on the router in the same way as we do on the express application.

The only difference is that we call them on the router variable and not on the app variable.

Make sure to pick router, followed by .get.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You define routes on a router as you do on an Express app. Use .get for a GET route.

Define only a GET route on router, and store the name in the variable used by the response.

Make sure to pick router, followed by .get, and finally user.

lessons.title: Lesson #4
lessons.interactiveContent:
The router allows us to group similar routes together and use them in the main app. We use a router as we use middleware with app.use.

We can now call http://localhost:3000/greet as we would when we directly define routes on the main app.

Make sure to pick app followed by . and then use, router.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A router groups similar routes. You connect it to the main app as middleware with app.use.

Connect router to the main app so its /greet route is available.

Make sure to pick app, followed by ., use, and finally router.

lessons.title: Lesson #4 - Copy - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
The router acts like a mini-application, allowing us to move it into its own file for better organization and improved readability.

In app.js, we import the router to integrate it into our main application.

Make sure to pick userRoutes followed by require and then "./userRoutes", userRoutes.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A router acts like a mini-application. You can move it into its own file to keep your routes organized.

In app.js, import the router from "./userRoutes" with require and connect it to the app.

Make sure to pick userRoutes, followed by require, "./userRoutes", and finally userRoutes.

lessons.title: Lesson #4 - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
Of course, to allow importing the router as module, we need to export a module.

Make sure to pick module followed by . and then exports, router.
lessons.hardModeContent:
To let app.js import your routes, use module.exports to export the object that defines /greet.

Make sure to pick module, followed by ., exports, and finally router.

lessons.title: Lesson #4 - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
Adding "/user" when integrating the router into the main application, prefixes all routes in the router.

The route defined as "/greet" in the router can now be accessed via "/user/greet".

Make sure to pick app, followed by ., and finally use.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A path passed to app.use prefixes every route in the router.

For example, the prefix /user makes /greet available at /user/greet.

Mount this router so you can access its /greet route at /account/greet.

Make sure to pick app, followed by ., use, and finally "/account".

lessons.title: Router in Files
lessons.interactiveContent:
Access the Express router.

Make sure to pick express followed by . and then Router, (, ).
lessons.hardModeContent:
Access the Express router.

Make sure to pick express, followed by ., Router, (, and finally ).

lessons.title: Lesson #12
lessons.interactiveContent:
What is the correct way to import a router in your main app file?

const router = require("./routerFile");import router from "./routerFile";

const router = require("./routerFile");.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A CommonJS file named routerFile.js exports its router with module.exports. Which line imports that router into the main app?

const router = require("./routerFile");const router = require("routerFile");const router = express.Router("./routerFile");

const router = require("./routerFile");.

lessons.title: GET Endpoint
lessons.interactiveContent:
Create a GET endpoint using the router.

Make sure to pick router, followed by ., and finally get.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Create a GET endpoint using the router.

Make sure to pick router, followed by ., get, and finally res.

lessons.title: Lesson #13
lessons.interactiveContent:
What type of request does router.get() handle?

GET requestsAll possible requests

GET requests.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You connect a router using app.use(router). It defines router.get("/profile", handler).

Which request reaches this handler?

A GET request to /profileA POST request to /profileA GET request to any path

Make sure to pick A GET request to /profile.

lessons.title: app.use()
lessons.interactiveContent:
Use the imported routes.

Make sure to pick usersRouter followed by app and then ., use, usersRouter.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Use the imported routes.

Make sure to pick usersRouter, followed by app, ., use, and finally usersRouter.

lessons.title: Lesson #14
lessons.interactiveContent:
What happens if you prefix routes in the router like in this example with "/user"?

All routes in the router will be accessible under the "/user" path, such as "/user/greet"The router will only accept requests that match the exact path "/user"

All routes in the router will be accessible under the "/user" path, such as "/user/greet".
lessons.hardModeContent:
The mounted router defines router.get("/greet", handler). Which URL reaches that handler?

/user/greet, because the mount prefix comes before the router path/greet, because mounting removes the /user prefix/user, because the router path is ignored

/user/greet, because the mount prefix comes before the router path.

lessons.title: Intro I
lessons.interactiveContent:
Now that we've covered the basics of Express's router object, let's explore some of its methods.

The Express Router allows us to divide our application into small, maintainable sections, each with its own routing. But there is more!

lessons.title: Lesson #4 - Copy - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
Let's make the Express app use our userRoutes router.

The router works as middleware itself.

Make sure to pick app, followed by .use, and finally userRoutes.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Let's make the Express app use our userRoutes router.

The router works as middleware itself.

Make sure to pick app, followed by .use, and finally userRoutes.

lessons.title: Lesson #3
lessons.interactiveContent:
Of course, we can use GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE, and more.

Make sure to pick get followed by post and then patch, delete.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Use get, post, patch, and delete for GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE requests.

For GET, send Returned!. For POST, send Posted!.

For PATCH, send Patched!. For DELETE, send Deleted!.

Make each route handle only its named HTTP method.

Make sure to pick delete, followed by get, patch, and finally post.

lessons.title: Lesson #4 - Copy - Copy - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
The router itself can also host middleware. For example, we can use the built-in JSON middleware to parse incoming body objects.

We do that by calling use on the router instead of the app.

Make sure to pick router followed by . and then use, express.json().
lessons.hardModeContent:
A router can host middleware to parse incoming JSON request bodies.

Call use on the router so /new can read JSON data from req.body.

Make sure to pick router, followed by ., use, and finally express.json().

lessons.title: Lesson #4  - Copy - Copy
lessons.interactiveContent:
Similar to built-in middleware, the router can use custom middleware as well. Let's make our router use the custom logRequest middleware.

Make sure to pick logRequest, followed by logRequest.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A router can use custom middleware as well as built-in middleware.

Define logRequest and make the router use that function to log each incoming request.

Make sure to pick logRequest, followed by use, and finally logRequest.

lessons.title: Lesson #5
lessons.interactiveContent:
A neat trick is to pass the middleware function directly to router.use.

Make sure to pick router.use, followed by (req, res, next), and finally =>.
lessons.hardModeContent:
You can pass a middleware function directly to router.use.

Register this function on the router, with the parameters it needs to call next().

Make sure to pick router.use, followed by (req, res, next), and finally =>.

lessons.title: Example: router.use()
lessons.interactiveContent:
Code the correct Express function at the end of the first route-level middleware function to allow the next middleware to execute.

Make sure to pick next followed by ( and then ), ;.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Keep both middleware functions on router. At the end of the first, call the function that continues to the second.

Make sure to pick next, followed by (, ), ;, and finally router.

lessons.title: Example: use()
lessons.interactiveContent:
Let's look at an example that shows how multiple routers can give Express apps a nice structure.

Make sure to pick studentsRouter, followed by use, and finally app.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Multiple routers help structure your Express app.

Import the teachers router, then connect all three routers directly to app, once each.

Make sure to pick require, followed by studentsRouter, use, and finally app.

lessons.title: Lesson #14
lessons.interactiveContent:
Can we handle multiple HTTP requests in a single router?

Yes, you can handle as many request types as you wantNo, we need multiple routers for that

Yes, you can handle as many request types as you want.
lessons.hardModeContent:
An API needs GET /books and POST /books. Can one router define both handlers?

Yes, with router.get() and router.post() on the same routerNo, each HTTP method requires a separate routerNo, the second handler would replace the first because both use /books

Yes, with router.get() and router.post() on the same router.

lessons.title: Lesson #12
lessons.interactiveContent:
How can you handle a DELETE request in a router?

By using router.delete("/path", handler)By using router.remove("/path", handler)

By using router.delete("/path", handler).
lessons.hardModeContent:
The API must delete the task identified by /tasks/:id. Which route handles a DELETE request?

router.delete("/tasks/:id", handler)router.remove("/tasks/:id", handler)router.get("/tasks/:id", handler)

router.delete("/tasks/:id", handler).
